sentences.text: Pelorosaurus is a genus of titanosauriform sauropod dinosaur, a name that translates to "monstrous lizard".
In life, this animal was a medium-sized sauropod compared to the giants of its group, reaching 16 meters in length, 4 meters in height, and weighing 17 tons.
The humerus measures 137 centimeters in length, suggesting relatively long forelimbs typical of brachiosaurids.
Pelorosaurus was the first sauropod to be identified as a dinosaur, even though it was not the first to be discovered.
Gideon Mantell acquired the large humerus used to describe the genus for 8 pounds.
Gideon Mantell identified Pelorosaurus as a land-dwelling dinosaur.
Mantell originally intended to name the genus "Colossosaurus" but changed it after learning that the Greek word meant "statue" rather than "giant".
The generic name Pelorosaurus is derived from the Greek word pelor, meaning "monster".
In November 1849, Mantell decided against the name "Colossosaurus" because he realized the root meant "statue" instead of "giant".

Mantell used both the sauropod material of Cetiosaurus brevis and a large humerus found by miller Peter Fuller at the same site, which he assumed belonged to the same individual and was discovered only a few meters from the vertebrae.
Richard Owen resolved the taxonomic issue by designating the humerus as the sole holotype for Pelorosaurus conybeari.
The type species P. conybeari was based on a humerus and vertebrae that were discovered separately.
The shape of the humerus, designed to support body weight vertically and possessing a medullary cavity, indicated that Pelorosaurus was a land animal.
The humerus, clearly formed to support the body weight vertically and presumed to possess a medullary cavity, showed that Pelorosaurus was a terrestrial animal.
Pelorosaurus became a "wastebasket taxon" used to classify various fragmentary European sauropods from the Early Cretaceous.
The species Pelorosaurus manseli is considered a nomen dubium and is now classified as Ischyrosaurus manseli.
The species Pelorosaurus humerocristatus is now classified as Duriatitan humerocristatus.
The species Pelorosaurus armatus is now classified as Oplosaurus armatus.
In 1882, Henri-Émile Sauvage first stated that Pelorosaurus belonged to the Sauropoda.
In recent years, the material of Pelorosaurus has commonly been placed in the broader group Titanosauriformes.
Pelorosaurus was historically a wastebasket taxon containing many poorly defined sauropods.
Pelorosaurus belongs to the family Brachiosauridae and may have only three known species: P. conybeari, P. humerocristatus, and P. mackesoni.
Pelorosaurus humerocristatus is now considered a synonym of Duriatitan humerocristatus.
Pelorosaurus mackesoni is a nomen dubium now assigned to the genus Dinodocus.
Pelorosaurus lived in England during the Early Cretaceous period, approximately 140 to 125 million years ago.

Pelorosaurus conybeari is the only known species of the extinct genus Pelorosaurus, a braiosaurid sauropod dinosaur that lived at the beginning of the Cretaceous Period, about 132 million years ago during the Barremian, in what is now Europe.
Pelorosaurus lived from the Tithonian to the Albian stages, between 145.06 and 110.1 million years ago.
In 2007, researchers Michael P. Taylor and Darren Naish proposed to petition the ICZN to make Pelorosaurus conybeari the type species and abandon the name Cetiosaurus brevis.
By 1970, researchers John Ostrom and Rodney Steel argued that Richard Owen's claim that Cetiosaurus brevis was a nomen nudum was an inadmissible attempt to change the type specimen.

Modern standards suggest that Alexander Melville's renaming of the sauropod bones was incorrect because Cetiosaurus brevis was still available and he should have designated the sauropod bones as the lectotype.

In 1970, John Ostrom and Rodney Steel argued that Owen's claim that Cetiosaurus brevis was a nomen nudum in 1842 should be rejected as a transparent attempt to change the type specimen, which is inadmissible by current standards.

However, according to the same standards, Melville's name change was also incorrect because the name Cetiosaurus brevis was still "available"; he should have simply designated the sauropod bones as the lectotype, removing the iguanodontian remains from the series of syntypes.
In 2003, paleontologists Upchurch and Martin planned to petition the ICZN to preserve the name Pelorosaurus conybeari and suppress C. brevis.
